text: Flow Designer & Automation showed you one spoke action dropped into one flow, and left it there. What that lesson didn't dwell on is that a Spoke is never just one action — it's a bundle of multiple, independently usable actions, each one wrapping a specific operation against the external system's API. That distinction matters once you're the one deciding which bundled action a given business process actually needs.

Take the real Slack Spoke as a concrete example. It ships actions like Post Message, Create Channel, and Invite User — three completely different operations, each its own action, each droppable into any flow entirely on its own. A flow builder who only needs to post a notification never touches Create Channel; they wire in Post Message and move on. Another flow, provisioning a project workspace, might use Create Channel and Invite User together without ever touching Post Message.

Here's the detail worth sitting with: a Connector Action is modeled exactly like any other Flow Designer action you met back in course 4 — it declares named Inputs and named Outputs. Post Message takes inputs like a channel name and a message body. Create Channel takes a channel name and a visibility setting. Invite User takes a channel and a user identifier. The flow builder wires values into those inputs and reads the outputs back, the same drag-and-drop experience as wiring any other flow step.

Underneath Post Message, the Slack Spoke is doing real work: authenticating against Slack, typically through an Authentication Profile configured once back in Chapter 3; formatting the request body the way Slack's API expects it; calling the correct endpoint; and parsing Slack's response into the clean outputs the flow builder actually sees. None of that complexity leaks out. A flow builder who has never read a line of Slack's API documentation can still post a message, create a channel, and invite a user, because the Spoke's author already did that research once and packaged the result as a reusable action.

As the admin or developer, you're the one who confirms a Spoke is licensed and installed, connects its Authentication Profile, and decides which of its bundled actions a given flow actually needs. You're also the one who notices when the bundle doesn't cover a use case — when none of Slack's shipped actions do what a business process needs. Next up: exactly that situation, and how building your own custom action solves it.
